name: Vibrosaun

lead: The Vibrosaun is a body-conditioning machine in which the user lies on a padded vibrating bed with circulating dry heat. Promoters say it approximates the effect of exercise without stressing the body, aiming at toning, perspiration and a smoother-looking skin and body.

It was reportedly developed in Australia by a team including a medical practitioner, chiropractor, osteopath, physiotherapist and design engineer. It belongs to the long lineage of vibrating exercise machines, from Gustav Zander's 19th-century devices to Kellogg's belt machines and 1950s reducing belts.

paras: Users recline on the bed and operate the controls themselves while vibration and dry heat run, with music and cooled air at the head in the manufacturer's description. It is offered at spas, clinics and health-farm style venues, sometimes alongside hands-on therapy.

Published information is largely promotional. General precautions for heat and vibration apply, and promotional material advises people with medical conditions to consult a professional. No independent trial of the Vibrosaun has been located.

angle.text: Users lie on the bed for passive vibration and warmth, aiming for toning, circulation and skin-tone improvements. The effects are those described by the manufacturer and dealers.

lead: The Vibrosaun is a vibrating, warmed bed sold as a body-conditioning system. A promotional description says it was invented in Australia by a team of a medical practitioner, a chiropractor, an osteopath, a physiotherapist and a design engineer who wanted a simple machine that simulates exercise without stressing the body [1].

Marketing claims include muscle toning, better circulation and skin tone, reduced cellulite, perspiration, relief of aches and relaxation, linked to vibration massage and dry heat that is said to widen blood vessels [1]. People use it to get passive 'workout' effects for body shape and skin.

It descends from vibrating exercise machines such as Gustav Zander's late-19th-century devices, Kellogg's 1927 'Battle Creek Health Builder' and the 1950s belts marketed for fat reduction, which fell out of fashion by the 1980s [2].

paras: The user reclines on a padded bed and controls the machine from within. It combines vibration, dry heat circulating over and under the bed, music and cooled, ion-charged air for the head, according to the promoter [1].

Swedish physician Gustav Zander devised early vibrating machines in the 19th century, intended as massage aids. John Harvey Kellogg promoted a version in 1927 at Battle Creek Sanitarium. Similar belts were marketed in the 1950s to reduce fat without exercise and appeared in TV comedies; they declined in the 1980s after their lack of fat-reducing benefit became clear [2].
The promoter lists relief of muscle and back aches, better circulation and skin tone, cellulite reduction, muscle toning, perspiration, weight control and relaxation [1].
